To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) for rank aggregation, the best approximation factor known for a polynomial time algorithm is 1.5, (ii) for the feedback arc set tournament problem, the best approximation guarantee known is 2, and (iii) for the correlation and consensus clustering problems, the best approximation ratio known is 3.

for all three problems we address, there is a simple and elegant algorithm that gives a constant-factor approximation, that the feedback arc set conjecture is true unless NP⊆P, and that the feedback arc conjecture is true even if we are allowed to add an additional edge to the tournament.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the design of simple, yet efficient, algorithms that aggregate inconsistent information.
the following fundamental question: How can we aggregate contradictory information to produce a consistent global solution?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for the problems we address, there is a single algorithm that is the best possible for all of them.
for all these NP-hard optimization problems, we obtain improved approximation factors by using essentially the same simple algorithm.
for all the problems we address, we either show improved approximation factors, or we show that the problem is hard to approximate, unless NP⊆ BPP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the problem of finding a globally consistent solution to inconsistent inputs is hard, but that there are simple algorithms that can achieve near optimal results.
we can now aggregate inconsistent information better than before and that it is unlikely that we can aggregate inconsistent information much better than before.
for the problems we consider, we can either get better approximation ratios, or we can show that no better approximation is possible unless NP⊆RP.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a very simple and general algorithmic framework can be used to obtain strong approximation guarantees for a variety of problems in the context of inconsistent information.
a simple algorithm, that is oblivious to the structure of the inputs and the problem, can be used to obtain improved approximation factors for a large class of optimization problems.
the same simple algorithm can be used to solve several seemingly unrelated problems with improved approximation factors, which we believe is a novel approach.
